main_text.p: videtur fluxiones excitare, eas tamè postea cohibet, & comprimit: verum caput implet. Sudor in primis labore ipsius corporis, deinde etiam, siccis sudationibus euocandus, frictio adhibenda. Moderandumque inter haec, ut uires coseruentur. Paulus Ægineta post internam curationē, uti balineo rectè suader. Nam ante plus aegroto officit, quàm prodest. Hinc addit smegmata ex decocto betae, aut fœnigraeci cum aphroni-tro, aut sapone, aut myrabolano, & quandoq; etiam psilotris. Deterget etiam portulaca cum aceto trita, & tenue semper uicū, & rumicis radices aceto coctae, & alumen cum sale, & sandaracha Graecorum, (quod iuniperi gummi dicitur) æquis portionibus in uino, & oleo lentiscino, aut eius penuria, mastichino. Sunt & fere infinita huiusmodi, quę ab eo traduntur libro quarto, de re Medica, quorum Cap.I.ὁμωνυμικὰ[?] uis, non parua est. Narrat Plinius libro Naturalis historiae Cap.Ivicesimo sexto, Ægyptios, quibus peculia re hoc malum erat, balnea ex sanguine humano parare ad medicinam: sed multis cōmentum hoc videtur, quòd haec nihil conferre satis sit probabile. page.notes: The margin at the right holds faint pencil marks and show-through (for example near the top right); these are not printed and are left out. The word after "quorum" is Greek, printed small; I could not read it letter by letter, so the transcription is a best guess and is marked [?]. The first note reads "Cap.I." and the second "Cap.I" as printed; the numeral is uncertain and is not marked further. The page ends mid-word: "nihil-" with the hyphen printed at the line end, and the catchword "omi-" continues it.
